name: Shenzhen and the Markets

claims.claim_text: Reference books collecting mobile-phone schematics and register maps for widely used chipsets sell in the Shenzhen markets for around $10, including register sets that the silicon vendors themselves do not publish; the same material can also be photocopied out of local libraries.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you go to Shenzhen and you pay, like, you know, $10 for, like, a book on mobile phones. And then it has all the schematics and all the register sets for just about every, like, say, Qualcomm or whatever chip
claims.speaker: Akiba
claims.episode_title: An interview with Akiba from Freaklabs - Dimissory Diagraphical Debt

claims.claim_text: Shenzhen's parts ecosystem is oriented to businesses rather than enthusiasts, which is what makes it the place to run an electronics business; hobbyist-facing districts such as Tokyo's Akihabara serve a different customer and carry different stock.
claims.quote_verbatim: So, Shinzen is catered towards business. So, if you're going to do, like, an electronics business, that's where you want to be.
claims.speaker: Akiba
claims.episode_title: An interview with Akiba from Freaklabs - Dimissory Diagraphical Debt

claims.claim_text: An injection mould for a modest product enclosure cost roughly $20,000 in the United States against roughly $5,000 in Shenzhen.
claims.quote_verbatim: depends wildly on, on where you're going, but, uh, stateside about 20 grand, uh, in Shenzhen about five grand
claims.speaker: Eric Van Wyk
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: Huaqiangbei, the wholesale electronics market in Shenzhen, runs to thousands of small stands across six floors of some twenty buildings covering a whole neighbourhood, with entire areas given over to a single category such as switch or connector samples.
claims.quote_verbatim: which has Hua Chongbei, which is, I guess, the world's largest wholesale part market. Mm-hmm. There's thousands of little stands covering six floors of 20 buildings. Oh. Uh, you know, over a whole neighborhood with nothing but switch samples and connector samples
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: The Huaqiangbei stalls are set up to serve manufacturers rather than individuals, but a hobbyist can walk in and buy small quantities from them anyway.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because most of them are intended for big manufacturers. But you can get in there as a hobbyist and buy things as well
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: A pogo-pin bed-of-nails test fixture with toggle clamps, the kind normally built in-house, costs on the order of $50 from stalls in the Chinese electronics markets that do nothing else.
claims.quote_verbatim: those test fixtures, they're like, they're $50 in China
claims.speaker: Akiba

claims.claim_text: The procedure for buying a test fixture in the Shenzhen markets is to carry the bare PCB to the stall that makes pogo-pin fixtures and mark the holes to be contacted with a red marker; no Gerbers or drill files are asked for.
claims.quote_verbatim: you just take your PCB to Shenzhen and you go to the stand, like the stand in the electronics market that does the Poga pin fixtures. And then you just, you just take a red marker and you highlight all the holes that you want the Poga pins to hit
claims.speaker: Akiba

claims.claim_text: Shenzhen supports hand-placement services where an operator buys the stencil, populates and reflows a handful of boards, and is paid a day's wage for the job, which comes out roughly an order of magnitude cheaper than setting up a machine line for three to five boards.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's this placement service in, obviously it was Shenzhen, but it was like a placement service in Shenzhen where, you know, they, they buy the stencil and they just, you know, they put together five boards and they'll reflow it, right? Right. And they're all oven. But it's just, you're paying someone just to do that all day long. And you can get three to five boards out of it and, but pay them for a day's wage

claims.claim_text: Stallholders in the Shenzhen electronics market generally do not speak English, but every stall has a calculator and everyone works from part numbers, so a purchase can be completed by exchanging a part number and a price.
claims.quote_verbatim: in the electronics market, um, people don't really speak English, but they all have calculators and they, and everybody understands part numbers
claims.speaker: Zach Hoeken
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Hoeken Smith - Creative China Commorant

claims.claim_text: Bringing a translator is the fastest way through the language barrier in the markets, at the cost that people who always bring an assistant tend to spend years in Shenzhen without learning any Mandarin.
claims.quote_verbatim: the easiest way is just to bring someone who helped you translate, whether that's a friend or like a coworker or an assistant. Um, or the, if, if you're kind of independent and you want to just do it yourself, because, uh, that's really the only way to learn and improve. I think, you know, if you bring along an assistant, you're going to be one and, and you're out here living, you're going to be one of those guys who's been here for five years and can't speak a word of, of Mandarin
claims.speaker: Zach Hoeken
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Hoeken Smith - Creative China Commorant

claims.claim_text: Roughly 80 to 90 percent of Shenzhen's population, in a city of about 20 million, leaves for Chinese New Year, and the airports and train stations become impassable during what is the largest annual human migration.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think it's 80 or 90% of the population of Shenzhen leaves for Chinese New Year. Uh, and it's a city of 20 million
claims.speaker: Scotty Allen

claims.claim_text: Brand representation in the Shenzhen gray markets is loose enough that sellers will peel the labels off generic resistor reels and apply a name-brand sticker in front of the customer, then ask about fifty percent more for the rebranded part.
claims.quote_verbatim: taking generic resistors, peeling the sticker off of them and then sticking on like a Samsung brand on them
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang - Bunnie's Bibelot Bonification

claims.claim_text: A common gray-market counterfeit is an entirely different die in a correctly marked package: a part marked LM741 that is actually an LM317 regulator, so the failure has nothing to do with the number printed on it.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're getting these counterfeit parts that just say, you know, if you're looking for an LM 741, assuming that everyone obviously probably won't. Uh, but you're just getting a chip now that says LM 741 and it's actually inside. It's some, you know, it's a LM 317 and you're getting a power regulator and, and, and you're up, you're up a creek
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Counterfeit parts span a range of origins: at worst a slug of metal in a marked package, more often dies that failed test on the genuine line, or authentic parts run on an unauthorised ghost shift and sold into the gray market.
claims.quote_verbatim: some as bad as just a chunk of metal with a package and silkscreen. Yeah. You know, and then some – the other ones are often potentially defects that came off the real line but are defective chips or even potentially gray market that were run on a ghost shift
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: The standard defence against unauthorised part substitution is an approved vendor list: passives can be left to the factory as long as they meet spec, while for a small handful of components the acceptable vendors are named explicitly.
claims.quote_verbatim: What you'd want to do to get around that is create an approved vendor list. So for some things, potentially capacitors, resistors, you don't really care as long as it's within spec. For other things, you probably care. For a small handful of components, you probably care a tremendous amount. And for that, you'd want to give an approved vendor list of what you'll accept
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: A counterfeit can be a chip of the correct footprint carrying fresh labelling to make it look genuine; X-raying a suspect batch revealed an unrelated die inside.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was a chip of the right footprint. It was just completely with new labeling on it to make it look like a genuine chip
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with the SparkFun Team - Efficacious Engineering Ensemble

claims.claim_text: Counterfeit electrolytics have been found as a large can containing a much smaller capacitor, so the part meets the mechanical footprint and nothing else.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was a picture of a capacitor. You know, it was, like, a 2200 microfarad... Or no, it was 68,000 microfarad. Yep. So, 68 millifarad, I think. And then they cut it open. And there was just a smaller capacitor on the inside, inside the casing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: An assembler substituting a surface-mount header with a cheaper plastic body produced connectors that melted and left pins at odd angles coming out of reflow; the substitution was invisible until the boards came back.
claims.quote_verbatim: one of the assemblers substituted a header connector, you know, one of these surface-mount header connectors, right? So, we got these boards back and all these connectors were all melted. And all the pins were all at weird angles because the plastic they used in these headers was just so crap. That was actually chocolate. Yeah. Yeah. And I've got a photo of this, you know, just totally distorted connector after it went through the reflow process
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Colin O'Flynn - Aspirated Adamantine Attacks

claims.claim_text: A connector body that cannot take reflow will nonetheless survive hand soldering, because only one pin is heated at a time and the housing never comes up to temperature, so hand-built prototypes will not expose the defect.
claims.quote_verbatim: Hand solder, they will survive just fine, you know, because you're only heating up a single pin at a time, you know, the whole thing doesn't have time to come up to temperature
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Colin O'Flynn - Aspirated Adamantine Attacks

claims.claim_text: Marking detail is what incoming inspection is for: a part branded as Infineon was caught because the manufacturer's name was misspelled by a single letter.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was branded Infineon. It's supposed to be Infineon, but it was Infineon, not O-N, but D-N
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Recycled parts sold as new arrive de-soldered with bent pins and solder bridges between them, evidence they were pulled off scrap boards on a hot plate, and are not worth the time to fit.
claims.quote_verbatim: sure enough, they come in and they're de-soldered. The pins are bent. There's shorts between, there's solder bridges between pins and they haven't even been nicely removed from the board. So it's like they're being removed on some hot plate, you know, some like fry pan or something
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Even a part as cheap as the 555 timer is counterfeited and marked as a major manufacturer's product, because the marking costs almost nothing next to the premium the brand carries.
claims.quote_verbatim: Not only are they fake, but they, they, they actually brand them as TI. They're like, they brand them as genuine TI. It's like, wow. Well, a bit of silk screen is pretty cheap
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The risk carried by a gray-market part scales with how hard it is to verify: an LED is tested by whether it lights, while a microcontroller can be wrong in ways no quick incoming check will catch.
claims.quote_verbatim: Well, some are higher risk than others, so, yeah. Yeah, if it's an LED, your test is, does it turn on? Oh, well, yeah, exactly. If it's an Atmel, like, 324 or something like that, you're a little more complex, right?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Cheap unbranded equivalents usually work well enough that buyers conclude they were fine, but they do not meet the genuine part's specification and tend to fail in the application where the margin mattered.
claims.quote_verbatim: in most cases they'll work, but they, they're not the genuine part. So they won't, you know, they won't perform the same, but in majority of applications, maybe that doesn't matter. You know, they, they work and people think, oh, AliExpress is good. I got them for half the price and they still worked. You know, and then one of them, and then one day you're going to come a gut. So when it's most critical, Murphy's going to get you
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A part listed around $1.50 at a Chinese catalogue distributor can be offered at $0.10 on AliExpress or Alibaba; that gap is itself the evidence the part is not genuine, and such parts have to be tested before they are assembled.
claims.quote_verbatim: even if you go to LCSC, right, they don't have any stock. But yeah, it's like $1.50 or something. But if you go to AliExpress, Alibaba, it can potentially be as little as $0.10, so they claim. But, you know, they're obviously not genuine ones. But you better test it before you put them in
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Chips that were once catalogue items increasingly reach independent repair only through unvetted brokers who cold-contact shops, so every lot has to be tested before it goes near a customer's board.
claims.quote_verbatim: the only place I could get this from is, you know, people Skype me saying, hi, I'm from China and I have this. And I'll wire the money and I'll, you know, cross my fingers and pray that what I get doesn't blow up the board that I'm working on
claims.speaker: Louis Rossmann
claims.episode_title: Right To Repair with Louis Rossmann

claims.claim_text: When a chip has no supply at any price, repairers buy complete assemblies for the one part they need, scrapping an entire iPhone XR charging case to harvest its ISL9240.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're actually at the point of buying charging cases because the iPhone XR charging case has an ISL 9240, ripping the chip off of it and then throwing it away
claims.speaker: Louis Rossmann
claims.episode_title: Right To Repair with Louis Rossmann

claims.claim_text: Long-lived defence programmes still buy 1980s-vintage parts through brokers, and those brokers source from individuals who stockpiled inventory decades earlier, which is the path by which counterfeits have reached aircraft such as the F-15.
claims.quote_verbatim: You know what the real problem there, I'm guessing, is an F-15 was designed in the 80s, and they're still buying parts from the 80s, and then their brokers go out. Yeah, their brokers go out, and they go and buy from that guy who stockpiled parts 15 years ago
claims.episode_title: Someone is watching...we think - Horme Hostility Hypochondriac

claims.claim_text: One practitioner defence against counterfeit components inside finished goods is to open the product first: taking SSDs apart to confirm the parts look legitimate before committing anything important to them.
claims.quote_verbatim: I do take them apart before I put them in to make sure that the parts look legit
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang - Bunnie's Bibelot Bonification

claims.claim_text: Market prices in Shenzhen sit far below retail elsewhere: a GSM-capable smartwatch and a Starbucks breakfast both came to about $9.75 there, and the same watch retailed for about $25 on Amazon.
claims.quote_verbatim: he said both of these cost nine dollars and 75 cents yeah right in shenzhen one of them has a gsm card and can talk to the network network rather um so there's a highlighted point here right so six dollars um well i've got nine dollars 74 at the market right so basically the uh it's the h6 smartwatch i'm sure yeah but there's a ton of these things so he was still only 25 bucks at amazon
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Shenzhen factories can copy a consumer product from its promotional video within days: a selfie stick built into a phone case was on sale on Alibaba at a fifth to a tenth of the creator's price before his thirty-day crowdfunding campaign had closed.
claims.quote_verbatim: before the kickstarter was even finished you could buy you know it was like 30 day kickstarter you could buy the finished product on em on uh alibaba you know for you know for like one tenth the cost of what he was going to sell it for
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Figures putting 80 to 90 percent of the world's electronics in Shenzhen circulate widely but are hard to substantiate, because the share depends on whether you count finished consumer assemblies or industrial equipment where only the boards are Chinese.
claims.quote_verbatim: I read in a Forbes article. 90% of the world's electronics comes from Shenzhen. I. That seems too high
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Chinese cities are ranked in tiers that broadly predict what industry is present: Shenzhen and Beijing are tier one, while a large city such as Chengdu with some electronics distribution is tier three.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's like a tier, I think a tier three, whereas Shenzhen and Beijing are tier one
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Shenzhen wage inflation was already running at about 13 percent a year while the region was still treated as the world's low-cost option.
claims.quote_verbatim: Wages are going up 13% in Shenzhen
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: DIP projects, OSHW & Trade Booths - Demonstrative DIP Dacrygelosis

claims.claim_text: Shenzhen's transformation falls inside a single working career: an engineer who first visited in 1987 recalls that the car she rode in was the only private car she saw in the city.
claims.quote_verbatim: The first time I was in Shenzhen was in 87. Yeah. And I think the car that I was in was the only private car I saw the whole time I was there
claims.speaker: Julia Truchsess

claims.claim_text: Shenzhen has hosted hardware accelerators that fly founders out for a roughly twelve-week programme ending in a demo to investors.
claims.quote_verbatim: Hexcelerator, the other hardware incubator, the one over in Shenzhen that we've talked about before, they are on their second round and they're looking for new applications. Sweet. So, people are interested. I mean, Bolt has been looking for people as well, but if you're interested in heading over to Shenzhen for, I think, 12 weeks
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Prototyping, Machining & Accelerators- Mugwumps Mulling Milling

claims.claim_text: The distinguishing service the Shenzhen ecosystem offered open-hardware projects was willingness to manufacture and fulfil batches of 100 to 1,000 units, a range most manufacturers will not quote at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: Especially for very small runs, which, you know, nobody's doing these tiny runs. And to have someone supporting open hardware with batches of 100 to 500 to 1,000 is just really excellent
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: Most listings on AliExpress and Alibaba are trading companies rather than manufacturers, the Shenzhen term for a middleman who buys to order or on spec, so a hundred apparent sellers commonly front a single factory.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of the things that you see advertised on like AliExpress and even to some extent on Alibaba, they're, they're not the manufacturer, right? It'll, they'll make it look like it. They're like a listing agent. Yeah. Yeah. Or what they, I think, you know, they're in Shenzhen, they call them a trading company

claims.claim_text: Because a product category usually has one actual maker, a buyer needing 3,000 units against 300 in stock has no second source, and a promised production run can still collapse when the maker cannot buy enough of its own microcontroller.
claims.quote_verbatim: if that company that makes it only has 300 in stock and you need 3000 of them, you're in trouble

claims.claim_text: Buying at volume out of Shenzhen effectively requires a local buyer who speaks Chinese and knows the manufacturers, because part selection there is an iterative negotiation across interlocking constraints rather than a catalogue lookup.
claims.quote_verbatim: having someone on the ground there, you know, obviously who speaks Chinese and knows all these different manufacturers is, is, it's just, it's just absolutely necessary

claims.claim_text: Silicon vendors gate application-engineering support by volume: a startup asking a major wireless vendor to open an account and speak to an FAE was told that without a commitment of 250,000 units a year no assistance would be provided.
claims.quote_verbatim: unless you can commit to 250 000 units per year um per parts or per product category or whatever i can't remember uh we won't be able to provide assistance

claims.claim_text: Early-stage companies without a recognised name struggle to get allocation from silicon vendors, which is what pushes them onto the Shenzhen spot market for parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: getting allocation of parts can, can be tough if, if you're early stage startup, if you don't have a big name, big name behind you. And there's always, there's always the spot market

claims.claim_text: When a mechanically critical part went obsolete and was only available from an unknown Chinese supplier, the workable answer was to pay a national supplier a premium to source and rebadge it, buying an accountable local counterparty rather than the lowest price.
claims.quote_verbatim: I was willing to pay a premium to a local company. A, you know, like a local, not even local, but like a national brand that could go, and I even sent them the webpage, and I'm like, you go deal with these guys. Right. You rebadge it with your label. You let me yell at you here in Cleveland, Ohio
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Cast-off assemblies from consumer products, such as iPad processor boards, are sold openly in the Shenzhen markets, and their substrates are far thinner than a standard board because they are the thin prepreg layers a multilayer stack-up is built from.
claims.quote_verbatim: a processor board from an iPad. They're just, like, cast-offs that you could buy in the markets of Shenzhen
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Chinese factories span an enormous range, from a cell where eight robots assemble a mouse around a lazy Susan with no human involvement to a third-floor walk-up with unlit stairwells where the wave-solder operator works in heels; seeing both ends is what teaches a buyer what is normal.
claims.quote_verbatim: we saw everything from really high-end, full automation, like a factory where they have a lazy Susan in the middle of eight robots that will assemble a mouse from components with no human involvement. What? Like, really... Did you hear that? And I was not allowed... I can't give you the name, and I wasn't allowed to take even stills. Yeah, I don't. To a third-story walk-up with no lights in the stairwells where the woman operating the wave soldering oven was wearing two-inch heels because she was going out that night
claims.speaker: Jesse Vincent

claims.claim_text: A local project manager with manufacturing experience earns his keep less as a translator than as a calibrator, able to say whether what the factory has just proposed is outrageous or simply normal practice in Shenzhen.
claims.quote_verbatim: I can turn to him and say, Ken, that sounds crazy, something the factory said. And either he'll turn to them and say, that's totally crazy and not acceptable, or he'll turn to me and say, no, Jesse, that's actually normal. Oh, really? Because, like, he has a lot of manufacturing experience. He knows not just what's normal for processes, but what's normal for processes in Shenzhen
claims.speaker: Jesse Vincent

claims.claim_text: Where labour is cheap relative to tooling, a factory will solve a part problem with people rather than a new mould: 5,000 RJ45 cables had their moulded locking-tab guards trimmed off by hand with a knife because that cost less than recutting the compression mould.
claims.quote_verbatim: they had assigned somebody with an Xacto blade to cut them off. Oh. So they've done 5,000 of them with cutting
claims.speaker: Jesse Vincent

claims.claim_text: Commodity-looking items shipped with a Chinese-built product, such as a short patch cable, are typically made to order rather than pulled from a shelf, so a change request is a change to somebody's process rather than a different catalogue number.
claims.quote_verbatim: all of these things get made to order. None of this stuff is off the shelf
claims.speaker: Jesse Vincent

claims.claim_text: The threshold for taking production overseas is better expressed in annual revenue than unit count: around a million dollars a year for a mid-sized Shenzhen ODM, far below what a Flex or Foxconn would entertain, and below that figure the advantage goes to a plant close enough to drive to and watch.
claims.quote_verbatim: our threshold is a million dollars a year. That's kind of, I think, low in our industry. Not ridiculously low but it's a lot lower than a large Flex or a Jable or Foxconn or someone like that would want to see. Below that, I think it makes sense to do it where, closer to wherever you are and, you know, drive over and, you know, watch the line yourself

claims.claim_text: Working in Shenzhen without Chinese is a genuine constraint rather than an inconvenience, because outside the expatriate circuit almost nobody speaks English.
claims.quote_verbatim: without any Chinese language skill you are completely lost even in the big city of Shenzhen almost nobody speaks English
claims.episode_title: Freelance PCB Design with Petr Dvorak

claims.claim_text: Shenzhen runs a shortage of qualified electrical engineers rather than a surplus, to the point that companies there outsource engineering work outward.
claims.quote_verbatim: they can't get enough qualified EEs in Shenzhen
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Wow, Dave REALLY likes Top Gun

claims.claim_text: A Chinese-language field guide to the Shenzhen markets, with the parts vocabulary printed in Mandarin so a buyer can point at it, is treated by regulars as basic kit for a buying trip.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're ever shopping in Shenzhen, you probably shouldn't go without getting this book, you know. Yes. I agree. Yep. Totally. I would not even hop on a plane there without getting this
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A common route into Chinese manufacturing is to find an existing similar product, in the markets or on Alibaba, and ask its maker to build a variant; the method breaks down only when nobody already makes something close.
claims.quote_verbatim: they'll find something similar and then they'll go find the manufacturer and be like, can you make something similar to, for me? And that's how people find stuff as well
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Inspirations and Aspirations - Recanting Rocket Rationale

claims.claim_text: The markets' advantage over any online catalogue is physical sampling: picking parts up and judging size, finish or opacity by hand, which is why buyers still travel rather than order remotely.
claims.quote_verbatim: that is the magic of the markets, you know, any, any place where like with that, where you have the hands-on, you know, just being able to pick stuff up and be like, click, click, click, click, click. Oh yeah. No, that, that's it. Or it isn't it. Or, you know, this is the right size or it has the right opaqueness that I'm looking for. Like there, yeah, I don't, I don't know, man. I think that, uh, in terms of like, like I agree with the library, but I don't know about the online stuff. I don't know if that's really possible. Uh, yeah, I think it's, it's just gotta be in person
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: Purely physical open-hardware products are readily replicated by Chinese manufacturers, sometimes at higher build quality than the original, which is the dynamic that undercut MakerBot and 3D Robotics.
claims.quote_verbatim: maker bot ran into trouble when there were Shenzhen copies of their hardware getting released. And decent ones. Right. No, no. Arguably sometimes better on the, you know, there were people who were, who were building really high quality products there

claims.claim_text: Contract manufacturers that guarantee against counterfeits do it by buying only through authorised distributors, and by refusing customer requests to source the same part more cheaply from consumer marketplaces.
claims.quote_verbatim: We try to buy everything through authorized distributors. And we pretty much hammer that home when people say, well, I can get this part cheaper on AliExpress
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: Consumables are counterfeited as well as silicon: fake soldering-iron tips for popular irons are widely sold through auction sites and perform badly enough to matter.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's a lot of fake parts out there, though. You've got to be very careful. A lot of fake tips and things like that that you buy on eBay
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: There is no established marketplace for reselling surplus semiconductors, so shortage-era stock changes hands through auction sites and brokers, which is exactly why parts bought that way are assumed to be fake.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's not really any resale markets that I know about though like because it's you know like it's it's kind of shady you'd have to sell them on you'd have to sell them on ebay

claims.claim_text: Suspecting that his distributors were simply buying in the Chinese market and reselling, one manufacturer concluded he would rather buy in that market himself, where parts can at least be inspected at the point of purchase instead of after shipping.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's what I suspect some of our distributors are doing, buying stuff in the market in China and sending it to us. Well, if, if, if they're going to do that there, I'll just do that here. And at least I'll know what, what, what brand they are. At least you can inspect them as you buy them instead of after, after they get shipped
claims.speaker: Charles Alexanian

claims.claim_text: For an instrument whose accuracy is the product, the deliberate choice was all-genuine parts and local assembly at higher cost, because the cheaper gray-market route yields fake parts that a precision design cannot tolerate.
claims.quote_verbatim: I made the commitment to, you know, use all genuine parts and have them assembled here in Australia, you know. Yeah. Cost more. Right. I could have gone to the deepest, darkest parts of Alibaba. Right. And, and, and tried to, you know, but you end up with fake parts. And when you're talking about precision parts like this, it just doesn't cut it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Chris Becomes Self Employed - Quixotic Quitting Quaere

claims.claim_text: Part-authentication schemes target a specific list of substitution modes: recycled components, unlicensed overproduction, test rejects, and outright clones.
claims.quote_verbatim: they claim it's for make sure it's not, they're not recycled components. Make sure they're not unlicensed over productions. Make sure they're not test rejects. Make sure they're not, you know, clones and copies
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Someone is watching...we think - Horme Hostility Hypochondriac

claims.claim_text: A pin- and code-compatible clone of a popular microcontroller is a counterfeit even when it functions correctly, and whether that matters is an application decision: tolerable in a novelty product, not in something whose failure has consequences.
claims.quote_verbatim: if it's an unlicensed chip, even if it's, you know, code and pin compatible, it's like, oh, that's just a counterfeit. You know, it just crosses that threshold. It's like, yeah, it's just like, that's just a fake part, but it just happens to work
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
